title: Introduction to Kubernetes
content:
Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform originally designed by Google and now maintained by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). It automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications across clusters of machines.

Kubernetes groups containers into logical units called Pods for easy management and discovery. It provides a declarative API that lets you describe the desired state of your workloads, and the control plane continuously works to make the actual state match.

## Key Features

- **Automated rollouts and rollbacks**: Progressively roll out changes to your application or its configuration while monitoring health
- **Service discovery and load balancing**: Kubernetes gives Pods their own IP addresses and a single DNS name for a set of Pods, and can load-balance across them
- **Storage orchestration**: Automatically mount storage systems of your choice—local, cloud providers, or network storage
- **Self-healing**: Restarts containers that fail, replaces and reschedules containers when nodes die, and kills containers that don't respond to health checks
- **Secret and configuration management**: Deploy and update secrets and application configuration without rebuilding images

## Architecture Overview

A Kubernetes cluster consists of a control plane and one or more worker nodes. The control plane components include the API server (kube-apiserver), etcd, scheduler (kube-scheduler), and controller manager (kube-controller-manager). Worker nodes run the kubelet agent and kube-proxy.

title: Installing Kubernetes
content:
There are several ways to install and run a Kubernetes cluster, depending on your use case—local development, testing, or production deployment.

## Local Development with minikube

minikube runs a single-node Kubernetes cluster on your local machine:

```bash
# Install minikube
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

# Start a cluster
minikube start

# Verify
kubectl get nodes
```

## Production with kubeadm

kubeadm is the official tool for bootstrapping production-grade clusters:

```bash
# Initialize the control plane
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16

# Configure kubectl
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config

# Install a Pod network add-on (e.g., Flannel)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flannel-io/flannel/master/Documentation/kube-flannel.yml

# Join worker nodes
kubeadm join <control-plane-ip>:6443 --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
```

## Managed Kubernetes Services

Cloud providers offer managed Kubernetes:
- **Amazon EKS**: Elastic Kubernetes Service
- **Google GKE**: Google Kubernetes Engine
- **Azure AKS**: Azure Kubernetes Service

Managed services handle control plane maintenance, upgrades, and high availability.

title: Quickstart Guide
content:
Deploy your first application on Kubernetes in under 5 minutes using kubectl.

## Prerequisites

- A running Kubernetes cluster (minikube or any cluster)
- kubectl CLI installed and configured

## Step 1: Create a Deployment

```bash
kubectl create deployment hello-k8s --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39 -- /agnhost netexec --http-port=8080
```

## Step 2: Expose as a Service

```bash
kubectl expose deployment hello-k8s --type=NodePort --port=8080
```

## Step 3: Access your application

```bash
# With minikube
minikube service hello-k8s

# Or get the URL directly
kubectl get services hello-k8s
```

## Step 4: Scale the Deployment

```bash
kubectl scale deployment hello-k8s --replicas=3
kubectl get pods
```

## Step 5: Clean up

```bash
kubectl delete service hello-k8s
kubectl delete deployment hello-k8s
```

Congratulations! You have deployed, exposed, and scaled your first Kubernetes application.

title: Pods
content:
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It represents a single instance of a running process in your cluster and can contain one or more containers that share storage and network resources.

## Pod Specification

Pods are defined using YAML manifests:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-pod
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "64Mi"
        cpu: "250m"
      limits:
        memory: "128Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
```

## Pod Lifecycle

Pods go through several phases: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, and Unknown. The kubelet monitors container health through liveness probes, readiness probes, and startup probes.

## Multi-Container Pods

Pods can run multiple containers that share the same network namespace and storage volumes. Common patterns include sidecar containers (logging agents, proxies), init containers (setup tasks), and ambassador containers (API gateways).

## Key Points

- Pods are ephemeral—they are not designed to survive failures
- Use Deployments or StatefulSets to manage Pods in production
- Each Pod gets a unique IP address within the cluster

title: Services
content:
A Service is an abstraction that defines a logical set of Pods and a policy for accessing them. Services enable network connectivity to Pods by providing stable endpoints, even as individual Pods are created and destroyed.

## Service Types

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `ClusterIP` | Exposes the Service on an internal IP (default) |
| `NodePort` | Exposes the Service on each node's IP at a static port |
| `LoadBalancer` | Provisions an external load balancer from the cloud provider |
| `ExternalName` | Maps the Service to a DNS name |

## Example Service

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 9376
  type: ClusterIP
```

## Service Discovery

Kubernetes supports two modes of service discovery: environment variables and DNS. The built-in DNS server (CoreDNS) automatically creates DNS records for Services. A Service named `my-service` in namespace `default` is reachable at `my-service.default.svc.cluster.local`.

## Endpoints

When a Service selector matches Pod labels, Kubernetes automatically creates an Endpoints object mapping to the Pod IPs. Traffic is distributed across healthy endpoints using kube-proxy.

title: Deployments
content:
A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. You describe a desired state in a Deployment, and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate.

## Deployment Manifest

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
```

## Rolling Updates

Deployments support rolling updates by default, gradually replacing old Pods with new ones. You can control the update speed with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`.

## Rollbacks

```bash
# Check rollout history
kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deployment

# Roll back to previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment

# Roll back to a specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment --to-revision=2
```

## Scaling

```bash
kubectl scale deployment/nginx-deployment --replicas=5
```

Deployments can also be configured for Horizontal Pod Autoscaling based on CPU utilization or custom metrics.

title: Namespaces
content:
Namespaces provide a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single Kubernetes cluster. They are intended for use in environments with many users spread across multiple teams or projects.

## Default Namespaces

| Namespace | Purpose |
|-----------|--------|
| `default` | The default namespace for objects with no other namespace |
| `kube-system` | For objects created by the Kubernetes system |
| `kube-public` | Readable by all users, reserved for cluster usage |
| `kube-node-lease` | Holds Lease objects for node heartbeats |

## Working with Namespaces

```bash
# List namespaces
kubectl get namespaces

# Create a namespace
kubectl create namespace my-team

# Run commands in a specific namespace
kubectl get pods -n my-team

# Set default namespace for kubectl context
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=my-team
```

## Resource Quotas

Namespaces can have ResourceQuotas to limit aggregate resource consumption:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: compute-quota
  namespace: my-team
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "20"
```

Not all resources are namespaced. Nodes, PersistentVolumes, and Namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped.

title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
content:
ConfigMaps and Secrets allow you to decouple configuration from container images, making applications portable and easier to manage.

## ConfigMaps

ConfigMaps store non-confidential configuration data as key-value pairs:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: "postgres.default.svc"
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  config.yaml: |
    server:
      port: 8080
      timeout: 30s
```

## Secrets

Secrets store sensitive data such as passwords, tokens, and keys. Values are base64-encoded:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
type: Opaque
data:
  username: YWRtaW4=
  password: cGFzc3dvcmQxMjM=
```

## Using in Pods

Both ConfigMaps and Secrets can be consumed as environment variables or mounted as volumes:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-config
    - secretRef:
        name: db-credentials
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-volume
      mountPath: /etc/config
  volumes:
  - name: config-volume
    configMap:
      name: app-config
```

## Best Practices

- Never commit Secrets to version control
- Use RBAC to restrict access to Secrets
- Consider external secret management (Vault, Sealed Secrets)
- Enable encryption at rest for etcd

title: List Pods
Create Pod
content:
Create a new Pod in the specified namespace.

## Endpoint

```
POST /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/pods
```

## Request Body

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `metadata.name` | string | Yes | Pod name (must be unique within the namespace) |
| `metadata.labels` | object | No | Key-value labels for the Pod |
| `spec.containers` | array | Yes | List of containers to run in the Pod |
| `spec.containers[].name` | string | Yes | Container name |
| `spec.containers[].image` | string | Yes | Container image to use |
| `spec.containers[].ports` | array | No | Ports to expose from the container |
| `spec.volumes` | array | No | Volumes to make available to containers |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X POST https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "kind": "Pod",
    "metadata": {"name": "nginx-pod", "labels": {"app": "nginx"}},
    "spec": {
      "containers": [{
        "name": "nginx",
        "image": "nginx:1.25",
        "ports": [{"containerPort": 80}]
      }]
    }
  }'
```

## Response (201 Created)

Returns the created Pod object with server-populated fields including `status.phase` set to `Pending`.

title: Delete Pod
content:
Delete a specific Pod from a namespace.

## Endpoint

```
DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/pods/{name}
```

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `namespace` | string | The namespace of the Pod |
| `name` | string | The name of the Pod to delete |

## Query Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `gracePeriodSeconds` | integer | No | Override grace period (default 30s) |
| `propagationPolicy` | string | No | `Orphan`, `Background`, or `Foreground` |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/nginx-pod \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

## Response (200 OK)

```json
{
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "kind": "Pod",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "nginx-pod",
    "namespace": "default",
    "deletionTimestamp": "2026-06-01T12:00:00Z",
    "deletionGracePeriodSeconds": 30
  },
  "status": {
    "phase": "Running"
  }
}
```

## Notes

- The Pod enters a Terminating state and is given a grace period to shut down cleanly
- Set `gracePeriodSeconds=0` for immediate deletion (requires `propagationPolicy=Background`)
- Pods managed by a Deployment or ReplicaSet will be recreated automatically

title: List Services
content:
List all Services in the specified namespace.

## Endpoint

```
GET /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/services
```

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `namespace` | string | The namespace to list Services from |

## Query Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `labelSelector` | string | No | Filter by label |
| `limit` | integer | No | Maximum number of results |

## Response (200 OK)

```json
{
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "kind": "ServiceList",
  "items": [
    {
      "metadata": {
        "name": "my-service",
        "namespace": "default"
      },
      "spec": {
        "type": "ClusterIP",
        "selector": {"app": "my-app"},
        "ports": [{"port": 80, "targetPort": 9376, "protocol": "TCP"}],
        "clusterIP": "10.96.0.12"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

title: Create Service
content:
Create a new Service in the specified namespace.

## Endpoint

```
POST /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/services
```

## Request Body

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `metadata.name` | string | Yes | Service name |
| `spec.selector` | object | Yes | Label selector to match target Pods |
| `spec.ports` | array | Yes | List of port configurations |
| `spec.type` | string | No | `ClusterIP`, `NodePort`, `LoadBalancer`, or `ExternalName` |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X POST https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/services \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "v1",
    "kind": "Service",
    "metadata": {"name": "web-service"},
    "spec": {
      "selector": {"app": "web"},
      "ports": [{"port": 80, "targetPort": 8080}],
      "type": "LoadBalancer"
    }
  }'
```

## Response (201 Created)

Returns the created Service object with `spec.clusterIP` assigned by the cluster.

title: Delete Service
content:
Delete a Service from the specified namespace.

## Endpoint

```
DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/services/{name}
```

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `namespace` | string | The namespace of the Service |
| `name` | string | The name of the Service to delete |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/default/services/web-service \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

## Response (200 OK)

```json
{
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "kind": "Service",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "web-service",
    "namespace": "default"
  },
  "status": {
    "loadBalancer": {}
  }
}
```

## Notes

- Deleting a Service does not delete the Pods it targets
- External load balancers provisioned by LoadBalancer-type Services will be cleaned up
- Endpoints associated with the Service are also removed

title: List Deployments
Create Deployment
content:
Create a new Deployment in the specified namespace.

## Endpoint

```
POST /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/deployments
```

## Request Body

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `metadata.name` | string | Yes | Deployment name |
| `spec.replicas` | integer | No | Number of desired Pods (default 1) |
| `spec.selector` | object | Yes | Label selector for Pods |
| `spec.template` | object | Yes | Pod template specification |
| `spec.strategy` | object | No | Update strategy (`RollingUpdate` or `Recreate`) |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X POST https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "apps/v1",
    "kind": "Deployment",
    "metadata": {"name": "web-app"},
    "spec": {
      "replicas": 3,
      "selector": {"matchLabels": {"app": "web"}},
      "template": {
        "metadata": {"labels": {"app": "web"}},
        "spec": {
          "containers": [{"name": "web", "image": "nginx:1.25", "ports": [{"containerPort": 80}]}]
        }
      }
    }
  }'
```

## Response (201 Created)

Returns the created Deployment object.

title: Update Deployment
content:
Replace an existing Deployment with an updated specification. This triggers a rolling update if the Pod template has changed.

## Endpoint

```
PUT /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/deployments/{name}
```

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `namespace` | string | The namespace of the Deployment |
| `name` | string | The name of the Deployment |

## Request Body

The full Deployment object with the desired changes. The `metadata.resourceVersion` field must match the current version to avoid conflicts.

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X PUT https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments/web-app \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "apps/v1",
    "kind": "Deployment",
    "metadata": {"name": "web-app", "resourceVersion": "12345"},
    "spec": {
      "replicas": 5,
      "selector": {"matchLabels": {"app": "web"}},
      "template": {
        "metadata": {"labels": {"app": "web"}},
        "spec": {
          "containers": [{"name": "web", "image": "nginx:1.26", "ports": [{"containerPort": 80}]}]
        }
      }
    }
  }'
```

## Response (200 OK)

Returns the updated Deployment object. If the image changed, the rollout status can be monitored via `kubectl rollout status`.

title: Delete Deployment
content:
Delete a Deployment and its managed ReplicaSets and Pods.

## Endpoint

```
DELETE /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/{namespace}/deployments/{name}
```

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `namespace` | string | The namespace of the Deployment |
| `name` | string | The name of the Deployment to delete |

## Query Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `propagationPolicy` | string | No | `Orphan` (keep Pods), `Background`, or `Foreground` (default) |
| `gracePeriodSeconds` | integer | No | Grace period for Pod termination |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://kubernetes.default.svc/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments/web-app \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

## Response (200 OK)

```json
{
  "apiVersion": "apps/v1",
  "kind": "Deployment",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "web-app",
    "namespace": "default",
    "deletionTimestamp": "2026-06-01T14:00:00Z"
  }
}
```

## Notes

- By default, deleting a Deployment also deletes its ReplicaSets and all managed Pods
- Use `propagationPolicy=Orphan` to keep the Pods running without management
- Deleted Deployments cannot be recovered

Create Namespace
content:
Create a new Namespace.

```
POST /api/v1/namespaces
```

## Request Body

| Parameter | Type | Required | Description |
|-----------|------|----------|-------------|
| `metadata.name` | string | Yes | Namespace name (DNS-compatible) |
| `metadata.labels` | object | No | Labels for the namespace |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X POST https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "apiVersion": "v1",

      "name": "staging",
      "labels": {"env": "staging"}
    }
  }'
```

## Response (201 Created)

```json
{
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "kind": "Namespace",
  "metadata": {
    "name": "staging",
    "labels": {"env": "staging"},
    "creationTimestamp": "2026-06-01T10:00:00Z"

  "status": {

```

## Notes

- Namespace names must be unique and follow DNS label rules
- Deleting a namespace removes all resources within it
- Avoid prefixing namespace names with `kube-`, which is reserved for system namespaces

- Binary data can be stored using the `binaryData` field

```json
}
```

title: List Nodes
kubectl CLI Reference
content:
kubectl is the official command-line tool for interacting with Kubernetes clusters. It communicates with the API server to manage resources.

## Installation

```bash
# Linux
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install kubectl

# Verify
kubectl version --client
```

## Essential Commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `kubectl get <resource>` | List resources |
| `kubectl describe <resource> <name>` | Show detailed info |
| `kubectl create -f <file>` | Create from manifest |
| `kubectl apply -f <file>` | Create or update from manifest |
| `kubectl delete <resource> <name>` | Delete a resource |
| `kubectl logs <pod>` | Print Pod logs |
| `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- <cmd>` | Execute command in container |
| `kubectl port-forward <pod> 8080:80` | Forward local port to Pod |

## Context Management

```bash
# View current context
kubectl config current-context

# Switch context
kubectl config use-context my-cluster

# Set default namespace
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=my-namespace
```

## Output Formatting

```bash
# JSON output
kubectl get pods -o json

# Custom columns
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase

# JSONPath
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
```

title: Helm Package Manager
content:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. It uses charts—collections of files that describe a related set of Kubernetes resources—to simplify application deployment and management.

## Installation

```bash
# Script install
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install helm

# Verify
helm version
```

## Key Concepts

| Concept | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Chart | A Helm package containing Kubernetes manifests |
| Repository | A collection of charts available for download |
| Release | An instance of a chart running in a cluster |
| Values | Configuration that customizes a chart |

## Common Commands

```bash
# Add a chart repository
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo update

# Search for charts
helm search repo nginx

# Install a chart
helm install my-release bitnami/nginx --namespace web --create-namespace

# Customize with values
helm install my-release bitnami/nginx -f values.yaml

# List releases
helm list --all-namespaces

# Upgrade a release
helm upgrade my-release bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount=3

# Uninstall a release
helm uninstall my-release --namespace web
```

## Creating Charts

```bash
helm create my-chart
```

This generates a chart directory with `Chart.yaml`, `values.yaml`, and template files. Helm uses Go templates to render Kubernetes manifests from chart templates and values.
